summary: Kastner's 1999 PNAS colloquium paper synthesizes how biogenic, authigenic, detrital, cosmogenic and hydrothermal oceanic minerals record seawater chemistry, ocean circulation, climate and the evolution of life. It emphasizes biogenic and authigenic minerals, describes their proxies (isotopes and trace element ratios), summarizes sediment sources and distribution, discusses economically significant minerals such as francolite and hydrothermal sulfides, and gives examples of rapid climate shifts and the Mediterranean Salinity Crisis. The text is truncated mid-sentence at the end.
one_line: Review of oceanic minerals (biogenic, authigenic, detrital, hydrothermal) as archives of seawater chemistry, ocean circulation, and climate change.
key_facts: Kastner's paper was presented at a National Academy of Sciences colloquium 'Geology, Mineralogy, and Human Welfare' held November 8–9, 1998 at the Arnold and Mabel Beckman Center in Irvine, CA.
Presently the best-developed geochemical proxies in biogenic carbonates include 18O/16O and Sr/Ca ratios for temperature, and 13C/12C for ocean productivity.
Marine barite is described as an effective alternative monitor of seawater 87Sr/86Sr, especially where carbonates are diagenetically altered or absent.
The first recovery of long cores on the Albatross Swedish expedition (1947–1949) revolutionized understanding of Pleistocene-Holocene ice ages recorded in oceanic minerals.
Cosmogenic particles entering the sedimentary record amount to about 4–6 × 10^4 tons per year.
Heinrich events involved pulses of massive detritus transport by icebergs from northeast Canada into the Labrador Sea and North Atlantic Ocean during glacial retreat.
Mid-Cretaceous organic carbon-rich black sediments are concentrated in the Aptian (115–110 Ma) and Cenomanian/Turonian (~90 Ma), known as the Cretaceous Anoxic Events (CAE).
Barite is the only mineral so far reported to also form in the water column.

Pyrite formation via bacterial sulfate reduction involves isotopic fractionation of about 40%, so pyrite formation modulates seawater sulfate sulfur isotopic composition and atmospheric oxygen content.
Oceanic phosphorites form more than 80% of the world phosphate, whereas guano deposits are considerably less economically important.
Hydrothermal sulfide deposits at the TAG area of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (~26°N) were drilled during Ocean Drilling Program Leg 158 in 1994 and have been forming for at least 20,000 years.
Estimates are that 2.7 million tons of massive sulfides exist above the seafloor and at least 1.2 million tons beneath it at TAG.
About 30% of the oceanic heat budget is removed by hydrothermal circulation.
The entire ocean volume circulates through oceanic basement at spreading centers in 5–7 million years.
The Mediterranean Sea almost completely dried up in the late Miocene Messinian stage 6–5 Ma when the Gibraltar isthmus tectonically separated it from the Atlantic Ocean.
